images.archetype: Circular vignette hero — composition H (Clinical), camera over-the-shoulder
images.placement: Hero, circular vignette beside the title (patient view)
images.alt_text: A Filipina in her forties sits with her nephrologist at a bright clinic desk, holding a 24-hour urine collection container while the doctor points to a kidney ultrasound image on a tablet

images.placement: Patients · Start Here — top, directly under the red emergency box
images.alt_text: Emergency warning card with icons: seizure, hand or face spasm, trouble breathing, fainting or racing heart, side pain with fever, little or no urine, and nonstop vomiting

images.placement: Patients · Start Here — after the four-word cards
images.alt_text: Three panels: a blood tube asking how much calcium is in the blood, a 24-hour urine container asking how much the kidneys release, and a kidney scan showing specks inside the kidney and a stone in the urine tube
images.status: Wired in guide (revised prompt — simpler wording)

images.placement: Patients · Low Blood Calcium — after the first paragraph
images.alt_text: Circular diagram of three helpers that keep blood calcium steady: parathyroid hormone from the neck glands, activated vitamin D from the kidney, and magnesium, acting on bone, kidney and gut

images.placement: Patients · High Urine Calcium — after the "Common drivers" paragraph
images.alt_text: Side-by-side picture of the kidney as a recycling sieve: normally almost all calcium returns to the blood, while salty food, lots of meat, excess pills or an overactive parathyroid let more calcium spill into the urine

images.placement: Patients · High Urine Calcium — inside or right after the myth box
images.alt_text: Myth versus fact: avoiding calcium lets more oxalate reach the urine and weakens bones, while calcium eaten with meals binds oxalate in the gut and protects bones

images.placement: Patients · Specks vs Stones — under the section heading
images.alt_text: Cutaway kidney contrasting fine calcium specks in the inner pyramids with a stone in the renal pelvis and another blocking the ureter, with a small kettle analogy inset
images.status: Wired in guide (revised prompt — adds kettle analogy)

images.placement: Patients · Tests — replaces or sits beside the 24-hour collection steps
images.alt_text: Five-step picture guide to a 24-hour urine collection: flush the first morning urine, write the start time, collect all urine day and night, keep it cool, and add the final urine at the same time the next morning

images.placement: Patients · Prevention — after the habits table
images.alt_text: Food chart of a stone-smart Filipino plate: keep milk, yogurt, small fish with bones, tokwa and water with meals; cut down patis, toyo, bagoong, instant noodles, processed meats and soft drinks; watch large meat portions and high-dose vitamin C

images.placement: Clinicians · Physiology — under the section heading
images.alt_text: Nephron schematic of calcium reabsorption in the proximal tubule, thick ascending limb and distal tubule, showing the calcium-sensing receptor, TRPV5, PTH and calcitriol regulation, and the opposite effects of thiazide and loop diuretics

images.placement: Clinicians · Hypocalcemia — replaces or sits beside the workup algorithm card
images.alt_text: Clinical algorithm for low calcium: emergency triage, confirmation with ionized calcium, magnesium correction, then classification by PTH and phosphate into hypoparathyroidism, ADH1, vitamin D deficiency, CKD-MBD or PTH resistance

images.placement: Clinicians · Chronic HypoPT — after the ESE table
images.alt_text: Balance-scale illustration showing that in hypoparathyroidism, raising blood calcium with tablets and active vitamin D increases urine calcium, with the ESE thresholds and the recommended responses

images.placement: Clinicians · Stone Risk Testing — after the context-threshold table
images.alt_text: Clinician reference card with a six-step reading order for a 24-hour urine and a table of context-specific urinary calcium thresholds from ESE 2025, AUA 2026 and EAU

images.placement: Clinicians · Nephrocalcinosis — under the section heading
images.alt_text: Diagnostic map pairing medullary or cortical nephrocalcinosis with laboratory patterns that point to primary hyperparathyroidism, vitamin D excess, distal renal tubular acidosis, hyperoxaluria, ADH1 or tubular disorders

images.placement: Clinicians · Acute Stones — after the imaging and analgesia paragraphs
images.alt_text: Clinical algorithm for an acute kidney stone: drain first if infection or obstruction red flags are present; otherwise analgesia, imaging, and alpha-blocker therapy mainly for distal stones larger than 5 mm, with urology referral when needed

images.placement: Clinicians · Prevention — under the section heading
images.alt_text: Clinical algorithm for calcium stone prevention: general measures for all patients, then a medicine matched to the 24-hour urine abnormality, then a repeat collection

images.placement: Clinicians · Absolute Effects — above the trials table
images.alt_text: Icon arrays for 100 people: a normal-calcium low-salt diet lowered five-year stone recurrence from 38 to 20, while hydrochlorothiazide (59 versus 49) and a hydration coaching program (20 versus 19) showed no clear difference

images.placement: Clinicians · Cases — under the section heading
images.alt_text: Three case cards: low blood and high urine calcium after thyroid surgery, suspected distal renal tubular acidosis with nephrocalcinosis, and a recurrent stone former with low urine volume and high sodium

images.placement: Clinicians · Physiology — after the Randall plaque paragraph
images.alt_text: Papilla cross-section in four stages: calcium phosphate plaque starts in the basement membrane of a thin loop of Henle, spreads under the urothelium, becomes exposed, and anchors a growing calcium oxalate stone, contrasted with crystal plugs inside collecting ducts
